article_title: Q-Learning Lab: Teaching Reinforcement Learning Through Learner-Generated Trace Analysis
citation: Jueng, Ekkachai. (2026). Q-Learning Lab: Teaching Reinforcement Learning Through Learner-Generated Trace Analysis. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10802
title: Q-Learning Lab: a single-file bilingual browser tool for teaching tabular Q-learning
description: Q-Learning Lab is a 'single-file, browser-based, bilingual (Thai/English) tool for teaching tabular Q-learning that requires no installation and no network connection.' It renders a 5×5 gridworld with color-coded Q-values and policy arrows, exposes a live Bellman-substitution panel showing the numeric update at every step, logs every transition with the full pre-action Q-row, and exports the trace as CSV for learner-side analysis.
requirements: Runs offline from one HTML file with no external dependencies; the article states it 'runs from a double-click on any modern browser'.
constraints: Tabular Q-learning on a deterministic, fully observable, single-agent gridworld only; stochastic transitions, function approximation, continuing tasks, and multi-agent settings are 'out of scope by design'.
target_learners: undergraduates in introductory machine-learning / reinforcement-learning courses
target_learning_goals: diagnosing agent behavior against the optimal policy
key_sources: Jueng, Ekkachai. (2026). Q-Learning Lab: Teaching Reinforcement Learning Through Learner-Generated Trace Analysis. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10802

article_title: Nursing competencies for family-centred care in the hospital setting: A multinational Q-methodology study.
citation: Hengeveld B, Maaskant JM, Lindeboom R, Marshall AP, Vermeulen H, Eskes AM. (2021). Nursing competencies for family‐centred care in the hospital setting: A multinational Q‐methodology study. Journal of Advanced Nursing, 77(4), 1783–1799. https://doi.org/10.1111/jan.14719
title: Ranked Q-set of 72 nursing competencies for family-centred care in hospitals
description: A ranked set of 72 nursing competencies for family-centred care in the hospital setting, developed through an integrative review and categorized using CanMEDS key concepts, then ranked by 69 Dutch and Australian professionals via online Q-sort. The article states "Our set of competencies can be used to guide education and evaluate practicing nurses in hospitals" and considers them generalist competencies each hospital nurse should have. The set overlaps the 2017 IFNA competency set, with 23 competencies the authors identify as new or markedly different.
requirements: Competencies were derived from published literature and validated for importance with lecturers, researchers, registered nurses and policy makers; family members were not included among raters
constraints: The article notes the comparison with the IFNA set was subjective because differences in descriptions made direct comparison difficult, and that reducing the number of competencies would very likely improve usability in research and practice
target_learning_goals: Family-centred care competencies: communication, collaboration, advocacy and partnership with patients and families
examples: Participants ranked the 72 competencies on an 11-column quasi-normal Q-sort table via a web-based system, with commentaries collected on their five highest and lowest ranked items
key_sources: Hengeveld B, Maaskant JM, Lindeboom R, Marshall AP, Vermeulen H, Eskes AM. (2021). Nursing competencies for family‐centred care in the hospital setting: A multinational Q‐methodology study. Journal of Advanced Nursing, 77(4), 1783–1799. https://doi.org/10.1111/jan.14719

article_title: Q-BEAST: A Practical Course on Experimental Evaluation and Characterization of Quantum Computing Systems
citation: Minh Chung, Yaknan Gambo, Burak Mete, Xiao-Ting Michelle To, Florian Krötz, Korbinian Staudacher, Martin Letras, Xiaolong Deng, Mounika Vavilala, Amir Raoofy, Jorge Echavarria, Luigi Iapichino, Laura Schulz, Josef Weidendorfer, Martin Schulz. (2025). Q-BEAST: A Practical Course on Experimental Evaluation and Characterization of Quantum Computing Systems. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.14084
title: Q-BEAST practical course on experimental evaluation of quantum computing systems
description: Q-BEAST is a lab course ('Praktikum') combining theoretical instruction with hands-on experimentation on real on-premise quantum systems at LRZ. The course is 'a combination of lectures, vendor talks, structured assignments, and projects', organized into four modules with seven assignments and two final projects, targeting benchmarking and performance evaluation skills. Students work in groups of two or three, with assignments taking one to two weeks and the final project three weeks.
requirements: Students access real quantum backends and HPC resources through the Munich Quantum Software Stack and work in groups of two or three
constraints: Class size was limited to a maximum of 15 students to manage workload and support, aligned with quantum resource allocation slots
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate students from computer science, physics, data science, and robotics
target_learning_goals: experimental evaluation and characterization of quantum computing systems
examples: Assignments include implementing a quantum circuit simulator, cross-entropy benchmarking, VQE hybrid molecule simulation, topology-aware qubit mapping, error mitigation, and pulse-level control; final projects are the Knapsack problem with QAOA and a QMMM workflow with VQE
key_sources: Minh Chung, Yaknan Gambo, Burak Mete, Xiao-Ting Michelle To, Florian Krötz, Korbinian Staudacher, Martin Letras, Xiaolong Deng, Mounika Vavilala, Amir Raoofy, Jorge Echavarria, Luigi Iapichino, Laura Schulz, Josef Weidendorfer, Martin Schulz. (2025). Q-BEAST: A Practical Course on Experimental Evaluation and Characterization of Quantum Computing Systems. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.14084

article_title: Q-BEAST: A Practical Course on Experimental Evaluation and Characterization of Quantum Computing Systems
citation: Minh Chung, Yaknan Gambo, Burak Mete, Xiao-Ting Michelle To, Florian Krötz, Korbinian Staudacher, Martin Letras, Xiaolong Deng, Mounika Vavilala, Amir Raoofy, Jorge Echavarria, Luigi Iapichino, Laura Schulz, Josef Weidendorfer, Martin Schulz. (2025). Q-BEAST: A Practical Course on Experimental Evaluation and Characterization of Quantum Computing Systems. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.14084
title: Weekly lecture-plus-assignment cycle with vendor talks and hypothesis-first experimentation
description: The course is organized into weekly meetings, each pairing an assignment with a relevant lecture or vendor talk, so that practical tasks build progressively on instructed content. Before conducting experiments, students are directed to develop hypotheses about expected results, which the authors state can 'help them improve analytical skills and get deeper into quantum principles'. Vendor talks from IQM, AQT, and planqc expose students to superconducting, trapped-ion, and neutral-atom technologies.
requirements: Access to real quantum systems and vendor collaboration for technology-specific talks
constraints: Students found lectures on ion-trapped and neutral atom quantum technologies challenging to follow compared with superconducting technology
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate students in quantum computing
target_learning_goals: connecting quantum theory to real-system experimentation
examples: Week one introduces Assignment 1 on quantum basics with an overview lecture; week two pairs a lecture on quantum circuit simulation methods with Assignment 2, building a quantum simulator
key_sources: Minh Chung, Yaknan Gambo, Burak Mete, Xiao-Ting Michelle To, Florian Krötz, Korbinian Staudacher, Martin Letras, Xiaolong Deng, Mounika Vavilala, Amir Raoofy, Jorge Echavarria, Luigi Iapichino, Laura Schulz, Josef Weidendorfer, Martin Schulz. article_title: Patients' Perceptions of Physicians' Health Literacy Competencies and "Good" Communication in Family Medicine: A Q Methodology Study.
citation: Tseng Pei-Ling, Yang Hui-Fang, Cheng Shao-Yi, Lai Hsiang-Ru, Huang Chiu-Mieh, Chen Jia-Yi, Tung Chen-Yin. (2026). Patients' Perceptions of Physicians' Health Literacy Competencies and "Good" Communication in Family Medicine: A Q Methodology Study. Inquiry. https://doi.org/10.1177/00469580251411672
title: 44-item Q-statement set and Q-sorting grid derived from the Physician Health Literacy Competency Indicators
description: A Q-methodology instrument of 44 statements converted from the Physician Health Literacy Competency Indicators developed by Liu et al through focus group interviews and the modified Delphi method. The indicators "were converted into Q-statements (Table 2) and arranged on a Q-sorting grid (Figure 2) following a quasi-normal distribution" on a 9-point scale from most important (+4) to least important (−4). Participants sorted cards in sessions guided by 3 trained research team members, followed by brief open-ended interviews, with sessions lasting approximately 30 to 60 min.
requirements: A statement explanation sheet with conceptual definitions and practical examples to ensure proper understanding of each Q-statement
Q-factor analysis software (PQ Method version 2.35) for factor extraction
constraints: The range of Q statements may not have encompassed all relevant factors
target_learners: family medicine outpatients as Q-sort participants
medical educators using the competency indicators
target_learning_goals: understanding patient perspectives on good communication
examples: 42 outpatients at 2 medical centers in northern Taiwan sorted the 44 cards; final arrangements were photographed and followed by two open-ended interview questions about the most and least important placements
key_sources: Tseng Pei-Ling, Yang Hui-Fang, Cheng Shao-Yi, Lai Hsiang-Ru, Huang Chiu-Mieh, Chen Jia-Yi, Tung Chen-Yin. (2026). Patients' Perceptions of Physicians' Health Literacy Competencies and "Good" Communication in Family Medicine: A Q Methodology Study. Inquiry. https://doi.org/10.1177/00469580251411672
